evidence.assay_type: clinical case report of allergic contact dermatitis
evidence.experimental_conditions: Propylparaben following use of Varicosan bandages
evidence.support_text: Lindner et al. (1989) reported a case of allergic contact dermatitis caused by propyl hydroxybenzoate (Propylparaben) following the use of Varicosan bandages. This represents a human sensitization outcome attributed to Propylparaben.

evidence.assay_type: Clinical observation of allergic contact dermatitis from occupational exposure
evidence.experimental_conditions: Vaccine contained 0.01% thimerosal; occupational exposure during vaccination of schoolchildren.
evidence.support_text: The patient developed allergic contact dermatitis on the hands due to contact with thimerosal during vaccination of schoolchildren, with vaccines containing 0.01% thimerosal.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Topical application of SADBE in acetone for treatment of alopecia areata; repeated application.
evidence.support_text: SADBE treatment caused eczematous reactions severe enough to require discontinuation in some patients, and one patient developed contact dermatitis on the arm due to transfer of the compound during sleep. These observations demonstrate skin sensitization (contact dermatitis) in humans.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 30 ppm formaldehyde; patch applied repeatedly for 1 week; 9 formaldehyde-allergic patients
evidence.support_text: Jordan et al. performed a double-blind controlled study on 16 formaldehyde-allergic patients. The closed patch test method showed positive reactions to 30 ppm formaldehyde in 4 patients.

evidence.experimental_conditions: not specified (reference to Levine 1960a)
evidence.support_text: The observation that groups of guinea pigs sensitized with PG or with BPE both give identical allergic reactions to patch tests with PG and with BPE indicates that the allergic contact reactions are specific for the diastereoisomeric benzylpenicilloyl groups.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 1% ethylenediamine dihydrochloride; 100 patients suspected of allergic contact dermatitis from topical medications
evidence.support_text: Fisher et al. (1971), in a study of 100 patients suspected of allergic contact dermatitis from topical medications, found 18% (18/100) sensitive to ethylenediamine dihydrochloride (1%).

evidence.support_text: Ethylene brassylate at 10% in EtOH:DEP was tested in diagnostic patch tests on 50 subjects (29 identified as atopics with sensitive skin) and resulted in 0/50 positive reactions (0%).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Latex or polyvinyl chloride gloves were ineffective barrier; exposure via occupational skin contact.
evidence.support_text: Only one case report, an electron microscopist, has been cited in the literature regarding allergic contact dermatitis as a result of exposure to vinylcyclohexene dioxide (VCHD). evidence.experimental_conditions: Occupational exposure as electron microscopy technologists; specific assay method not described.

evidence.experimental_conditions: 27,230 patients with chronic skin problems, patch testing with parabens at 1–30%
evidence.support_text: CIR (2019) reported that parabens can induce contact allergy, mainly after application of paraben-containing medicaments to damaged or broken skin. Even in patients with chronic dermatitis, less than 3% were sensitized. Of 27,230 patients with chronic skin problems, 2.2% were sensitized by parabens at concentrations of 1–30%.

evidence.assay_type: human clinical exposure and diagnostic patch test
evidence.experimental_conditions: Two exposures to 5% TP in OA/PG separated by approximately 3 months; diagnostic patch testing
evidence.support_text: Of six test subjects exposed twice to 5% TP in OA/PG in the PK study, five showed suggestive evidence of having become sensitized. The patch test results were interpreted as indicative of induced allergic contact sensitization to the TP/OA/PG formulation.

Three women were reported to have acute allergic contact dermatitis after using the topical pure oil of N. sativa extract (90). This constitutes a human adverse outcome of skin sensitization attributed to Nigella sativa seed oil extract.

evidence.assay_type: human clinical observation of contact dermatitis
evidence.experimental_conditions: topical application via cosmetic product; storage condition allowed oxidation
evidence.support_text: In 1992, an 'epidemic outbreak' of approximately 1,000 cases of allergic papular and follicular contact dermatitis caused by α-tocopherol linoleate in a cosmetic line was reported in Switzerland. The authors found that this compound was easily oxidized under the storage condition used. Therefore, secondary or tertiary oxidation products of α-tocopherol linoleate, rather than the reduced vitamin E ester, are likely to have caused irritation or even the oxidation of proteins and subsequent hapten formation.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Topical application of mechlorethamine solution to patients with severe alopecia areata; concentration not specified in the provided text.
evidence.support_text: Eleven patients with severe alopecia areata (localized and totalis types) were treated with topically applied nitrogen mustard. Two patients had an allergic contact dermatitis reaction to the mechlorethamine solution; no systemic side effects were seen.

evidence.experimental_conditions: occupational exposure
evidence.support_text: Isothiazolinones were shown to cause severe contact dermatitis and allergy in humans mainly with a high level of occupational exposure.

evidence.experimental_conditions: General clinic population
evidence.support_text: The potential of benzoyl peroxide to sensitize the patient and produce contact allergy has been vastly overstated. This incidence compares to the 1 to 2.5% reported by Pace (1965) and, interestingly, all of our cases, as those in his series, were women.

evidence.experimental_conditions: Occupational exposure to GENA

evidence.support_text: Eugenol, a frequent sensitizer, does not sensitize CYP1A1 knockout mice, whereas the wild-type mice are sensitized to eugenol. This indicates that CYP1A1 is responsible for generating from eugenol the ultimately antigenic metabolite(s) (Basketter et al. 2008).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Wild-type vs CYP1A1-knockout mice; topical eugenol treatment; sensitization observed in wild-type but not knockout mice.
evidence.support_text: Basketter et al. (2008) concluded that CYP1A1 converts eugenol to a sensitizing metabolite based on the observation that CYP1A1-knockout mice are not sensitized by eugenol, implying that wild-type mice are sensitized.

evidence.experimental_conditions: mice local lymph node assay (Hilton et al., 1996)
evidence.support_text: Eugenol was reported as positive for skin sensitisation in the mice local lymph node assay (Hilton et al., 1996).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Mouse (Mus musculus), vehicle-treated controls, test concentrations 10–50% for eugenol, vehicle not specified.
evidence.support_text: In contrast to the situation in guinea pigs, a significant degree of sensitization to eugenol was induced in the mouse, i.e., a dose dependent increase in proliferation and at least one test concentration inducing a 3-fold or greater increase (SI value ≥ 3) in isotope incorporation compared with vehicle-treated controls. Higher concentrations were used for eugenol (10–50%) than for isoeugenol (2.5–10%).

evidence.experimental_conditions: Mouse (Mus musculus), vehicle-treated controls, test concentrations 2.5–10% for isoeugenol, vehicle not specified.
evidence.support_text: It can be inferred that isoeugenol is actually a stronger sensitizer than eugenol in the mouse, but the difference is less than in the guinea pig. Higher concentrations were used for eugenol (10–50%) and its derivatives than for isoeugenol (2.5–10%) and its derivatives.

evidence.experimental_conditions: maximum allowed concentration of eugenol in a leave-on product; applied for 4 weeks; 5 volunteers previously sensitised to eugenol
evidence.support_text: Svedman et al. evaluated eugenol in a repeat open application test (ROAT) for a leave-on product. Five volunteers previously sensitised to eugenol were included, and the maximum allowed concentration of eugenol was applied for 4 weeks. Four of the five volunteers reacted, confirming the ability of eugenol to cause contact dermatitis [129].
